nodes.label: Human Evolution
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: The process by which modern humans (Homo sapiens) developed from earlier primates over millions of years. Africa is considered the cradle of humankind. Evidence comes from fossils, stone tools, and cave art. Key stages include Australopithecus, Homo habilis, Homo erectus, and Homo sapiens.

nodes.label: Australopithecus
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Early hominid genus that lived in Africa around 4-2 million years ago. Bipedal but with smaller brain capacity than later humans. The famous fossil 'Lucy' (Australopithecus afarensis) was discovered in Ethiopia in 1974. They were not tool-makers in the systematic sense.

nodes.label: Homo habilis
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: The first real 'Homo' or human (hence 'habilis' = 'handy/skilful'). Lived in eastern and southern Africa about 2.6–1.5 million years ago. First real stone-tool maker — fractured pieces of stone and sharpened them to use as tools. Fractured stones have been found alongside Homo habilis bones. Braincase 500–700 cc, lightly built.

nodes.label: Homo erectus
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Human species that lived roughly 1.8 million to 200,000 years ago. Braincase 800–1200 cc (vs Homo habilis 500–700 cc). First hominid to make the hand axe — the most distinctive tool of the species. Credited with the discovery and controlled use of fire, which enabled warmth in cold climates, protection from predators, and wider geographical expansion. First hominid to migrate out of Africa — remains found in China, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.

nodes.label: Homo sapiens
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Modern humans. Archaic Homo sapiens appears around 230,000–30,000 years ago (resembling Neanderthals, found in Europe, Near East, Old World). Full modern Homo sapiens sapiens traceable to ~115,000 years ago in southern Africa, in the Upper Palaeolithic. Braincase 1200–2000 cc. In India: Hathnora (Narmada valley) skull (found 1982) is archaic Homo sapiens; Fa Hien Cave (Sri Lanka) has modern Homo sapiens sapiens fossils ~34,000 years old. Earliest modern humans reached India via coastal migration from Africa ~50,000 years ago (from the south, not the north).

nodes.label: Neanderthals
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Species of archaic humans (Homo neanderthalensis) who lived in Europe and western Asia from about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. Had large brains, made sophisticated tools, and buried their dead. Went extinct after Homo sapiens arrived in Europe, though some interbreeding occurred.

nodes.label: Africa as Cradle of Humankind
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Africa is where the earliest hominids evolved and where the oldest fossils have been found. Key sites include Olduvai Gorge (Tanzania), Hadar (Ethiopia), and Sterkfontein (South Africa). The 'Out of Africa' theory holds that Homo sapiens originated in Africa and then migrated globally.

nodes.label: Olduvai Gorge
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Archaeological site in Tanzania's Great Rift Valley, one of the most important sites for understanding human evolution. Louis and Mary Leakey discovered fossils of early hominids here. Rich in stone tools from Oldowan and Acheulian traditions spanning 2 million years.

nodes.label: Stone Tool Traditions
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Three major stone-tool traditions in India, each tied to a Palaeolithic phase: Oldowan (simple flaked pebbles, from 2.6 MYA globally), Acheulian (hand axes and cleavers, from 1.7 MYA), and Middle/Upper Palaeolithic blade-and-burin industries. Neolithic stone tools are distinct — polished axes and implements — with three Indian regional types by axe shape: NW rectangular+curved-edge, NE rectangular-butt+shouldered, Southern oval+pointed. Parashurama, the axe-wielding legendary hero, is a cultural echo of this.

nodes.label: Neolithic Revolution
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Transition from hunting-gathering to agriculture and settled life, beginning around 10,000 BCE. First occurred in the Fertile Crescent (West Asia). Led to domestication of plants and animals, permanent settlements, pottery, and eventually urbanisation. One of the most transformative changes in human history.

nodes.label: Cave Art
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Paintings and engravings made by early Homo sapiens in caves, dating from about 40,000 years ago. Famous sites include Lascaux and Chauvet (France) and Altamira (Spain). Depicted animals, hunting scenes, and abstract symbols. Suggests symbolic thinking, ritual, and aesthetic sense.

nodes.label: Lascaux Cave
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Prehistoric cave in southwestern France containing some of the most famous Palaeolithic cave paintings, dating to about 17,000 years ago. Features over 600 paintings of animals including horses, deer, and bulls. Discovered in 1940.

nodes.label: Lucy (Fossil)
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: A remarkably complete Australopithecus afarensis fossil discovered in Hadar, Ethiopia in 1974 by Donald Johanson. Dated to approximately 3.2 million years ago. About 40% of skeleton was recovered, showing bipedal locomotion. One of the most famous fossils in palaeoanthropology.

nodes.label: Out of Africa Theory
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Theory that modern Homo sapiens evolved in Africa and then migrated to other continents, replacing earlier hominid populations. Supported by genetic evidence (mitochondrial DNA). Contrasts with the multiregional hypothesis which posits parallel evolution in different regions.

nodes.label: Origins of Language
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Language is considered a defining feature of Homo sapiens. Earlier estimated ~35,000 BCE; now pushed back to ~50,000 BCE (per Sharma, Upper Palaeolithic). Made possible by anatomical changes in the vocal tract and brain development. Probably facilitated the formation of bands and alliances among Upper Palaeolithic hunter-gatherers.

nodes.label: Controlled Use of Fire
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Evidence of controlled fire use dates to about 1 million years ago, associated with Homo erectus. Fire provided warmth, protection from predators, enabled cooking (which improved nutrition), and became a social focus. Cooking may have contributed to brain development.

nodes.label: Sulaiman and Kirthar Hills
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Hills in the northwest of the subcontinent where women and men first began to grow crops such as wheat and barley about 8000 years ago. Early agriculture also involved rearing of sheep, goat and cattle.

nodes.label: Hunter-Gatherers
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail:
Earliest people of the subcontinent who hunted wild animals and gathered plant produce for food. They lived along rivers and in rock shelters, moving from place to place following resources.

[merged from hist_hunting_gathering]: The primary mode of subsistence for most of human history. Groups were small, mobile, and egalitarian. Division of labour existed, with gathering (often by women) providing majority of food. Knowledge of environment, seasons, and animal behaviour was crucial.

nodes.label: Beginning of Agriculture
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Fundamental shift from gathering to producing food. In India: plant cultivation began ~7000–6000 BCE in the Sulaiman-Kirthar area and Rajasthan (Sambhar salt lake). Mature farming settlement at Mehrgarh from ~7000 BCE with wheat and barley. Animal rearing followed at Bagor and Adamgarh ~5000 BCE. By the Neolithic phase proper, settled agricultural villages spread across Kashmir, the Vindhyas, south India, and eastern India.

nodes.label: Mesolithic
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Middle Stone Age. In India, ~9000–4000 BCE. Transitional phase between Palaeolithic and Neolithic. Characteristic tools: microliths (tiny stone tools fitted onto bone/wood handles to make composite tools like saws and sickles). Post-ice-age climate warmer and wetter. People lived on hunting, fishing, and food gathering, and at later stages also domesticated animals. Key sites: Bagor (Rajasthan, occupied 5 millennia from 5000 BCE onwards, well-excavated), Adamgarh (MP). Bagor + Adamgarh provide the earliest evidence of animal domestication in India (~5000 BCE). Mesolithic sites abound in Rajasthan, southern UP, central and eastern India, and south of the Krishna river.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Neolithic
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: New Stone Age. Globally begins ~9000 BCE in western Asia; in India starts ~7000 BCE (Mehrgarh). North-Indian Vindhyan Neolithic sites ~5000 BCE; south-Indian Neolithic 2400–1000 BCE. Tools: polished stone axes and implements. Three Indian Neolithic regional groups based on axe types: (1) NW: rectangular axes with curved cutting edge (Baluchistan + Kashmir); (2) NE: rectangular-butt polished axes, occasional shouldered hoes (Vindhyas, Assam, Meghalaya); (3) Southern: oval sides, pointed butt (Karnataka/AP/TN, 850+ settlements). Neolithic innovations: polished stone tools, agriculture (wheat, barley, rice, ragi, horse gram), settled villages, domesticated animals, pottery (handmade → foot-wheel), mud/reed houses. Parashurama, the axe-wielding hero in Indian legend, symbolically links to the stone axe.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Microliths
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Tiny stone tools characteristic of the Mesolithic period. They were probably stuck on handles of bone or wood to make composite tools such as saws and sickles for harvesting wild grasses.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Bhimbetka
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: A prehistoric site in the Vindhyan range, 45 km south of Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh — over 500 painted rock shelters distributed across about 10 sq km. Discovered by V.S. Wakankar in 1957-58. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2003). Oldest paintings ~30,000 years old. Continuity of occupation from 100,000 BCE to 1000 CE — with paintings layered over each other across periods. Paintings span Upper Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Chalcolithic, early historic and medieval periods — most are Mesolithic. Called 'Zoo Rock Shelter' for depictions of bison, elephant, rhinoceros, tiger, cattle, snake, spotted deer, barasingha. Also shows Lower Palaeolithic stone-tool features in the lower layers. Themes: hunting, dancing, music, everyday life. Pigments: haematite (red ochre), purple, brown, white, yellow, green.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Hunsgi
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: An early Palaeolithic site in Karnataka where a large number of tools were found. Most tools were made from locally available limestone. Sites included both habitation and factory sites near springs.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Factory Sites
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Places where good quality stone was found and where people made tools. Identified by blocks of stone, discarded imperfect tools and chips of waste stone. Some were habitation-cum-factory sites.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Rock Paintings
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Paintings on rock surfaces made by prehistoric people, found at many Indian sites. Rock engravings (as distinct from paintings) are called Petroglyphs. Three major phases identified in Indian rock art: (1) Upper Palaeolithic (40,000–10,000 BCE) — large animals (bison, elephant, rhino, tiger); white/dark red/green for animals, red for hunters, green for dancers. (2) Mesolithic (10,000–4,000 BCE) — smaller paintings, predominantly red; group hunting, grazing, riding scenes. (3) Chalcolithic — increased green and yellow; battle scenes, men on horses/elephants, bow-and-arrow. Key sites: Bhimbetka (MP), Jogimara (Chhattisgarh), Mirzapur (UP), Panchmarhi/Pachmarhi (MP), Narsinghgarh (MP). Pigments from natural minerals — haematite (red), ochre/geru, lime. Bhimbetka was discovered by V.S. Wakankar in 1957-58.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Climate Change 12,000 Years Ago
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Around 12,000 years ago major climate changes led to warmer conditions, development of grasslands, and increase in deer, antelope, goat, sheep and cattle. Led people to think about herding and farming.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Habitation Sites
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Places where people lived, including natural caves and rock shelters found in the Vindhyas and Deccan plateau. People chose these for shelter from rain, heat and wind.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Wild Grain-Bearing Grasses
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Wheat, barley and rice grew naturally in different parts of the subcontinent. People collected these grains as food and gradually learnt to cultivate them, leading to the beginnings of agriculture.
nodes.chapter_title: On the Trail of the Earliest People

nodes.label: Domestication
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: The process by which people grow plants and keep animals. Began globally around 12,000 years ago. In India: earliest plant cultivation evidence from Sambhar (Rajasthan salt-lake deposits) ~7000–6000 BCE; earliest animal domestication from Bagor (Rajasthan) and Adamgarh (MP) ~5000 BCE. At Mehrgarh (c. 7000 BCE), domesticated wheat, barley, cattle, sheep, goats. Selective breeding made domesticated plants and animals different from their wild counterparts.

nodes.label: Mehrgarh
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: One of the earliest known farming settlements (c. 7000 BCE), on the Bolan river in the Kochi plain of Baluchistan — the 'bread basket of Baluchistan', on the edge of the Indus plains. Called one of the largest Neolithic settlements between the Indus and the Mediterranean. Grew wheat and barley from the outset; domesticated cattle, sheep, and goats (goats predominated initially, then cattle outnumbered others). Compartmented mud-brick granaries; rectangular mud-brick houses. Disrupted by floods ~5500 BCE, agriculture resumed ~5000 BCE. Potter's wheel introduced ~4500 BCE (from western Asia); pottery rapidly multiplied and was painted. Agricultural expansion into the Indus plain 4500–3500 BCE paved the way for the Harappan culture. In the dried Hakra basin (a tributary of the Indus), 47 Later Neolithic settlements have been found.

nodes.label: Burzahom
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: A Neolithic site in Kashmir, 16 km north-west of Srinagar. The name means 'place of birch'. People lived in pit-houses dug into the ground with steps leading in, on a lake-side; hunting/fishing economy with some agriculture. Earliest date ~2700 BCE. Coarse grey pottery, polished stone tools, extensive bone tools (made from antlers). The Kashmiri Neolithic is distinguished by pit dwellings, wide ceramic range, and the complete absence of microliths. Unique to Burzahom among Indian Neolithic sites: domestic dogs were buried with their masters in their graves.

nodes.label: Daojali Hading
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: A Neolithic site on the hills near the Brahmaputra Valley, close to routes into China and Myanmar. Stone tools including mortars and pestles found, along with jadeite possibly from China and fossil wood tools.

nodes.label: Pit Houses
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Houses dug into the ground with steps leading into them, found at sites like Burzahom in Kashmir. May have provided shelter in cold weather. Represent early settled architecture.

nodes.label: Neolithic Tools
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Polished stone tools with fine cutting edges, including mortars and pestles for grinding grain. Different from earlier Palaeolithic tools. Some tools were also made of bone.

nodes.label: Earliest Domesticated Crops
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Wheat and barley were among the first plants to be domesticated. Rice was grown in areas north of the Vindhyas. Millets were cultivated in southern India. Different crops suited different climates.

nodes.label: Earliest Domesticated Animals
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Dog was the first animal to be tamed. Sheep and goat were among the earliest domesticated animals. Cattle, pigs and buffalo were also reared. They provided milk, meat and served as stores of food.

nodes.label: Tribal Societies
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Groups of families forming a tribe, usually two to three generations living together. Land, forests and water were shared wealth. No sharp rich-poor differences. Women did most agricultural work.

nodes.label: Pottery
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Pottery first appears in the Neolithic phase when settled communities needed containers for storing, cooking, eating, drinking grains. Initially handmade; potter's wheel appeared at Mehrgarh ~4500 BCE (from western Asia), then spread across the subcontinent. Indian Neolithic pottery types: black-burnished ware, grey ware, mat-impressed ware. Painted pottery becomes common from ~2000 BCE onwards (Chalcolithic).

nodes.label: Koldihwa
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: A Neolithic site in present-day Uttar Pradesh where evidence of rice cultivation and fragmentary animal bones was found. One of the important early farming sites in the subcontinent.

nodes.label: Chirand
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: A Neolithic site 40 km west of Patna on the northern bank of the Ganges, at the junction of four rivers — Ganges, Son, Gandak, and Ghaghra. Open-land availability made settlement possible despite the riverine tract's paucity of stone. Distinguished by extensive bone and antler implements (from deer horns) — one of only two Indian Neolithic sites with a significant bone-tool industry (the other being Burzahom). Late Neolithic dates ~2000 BCE, possibly late Neolithic phase. Wheat, green gram, barley, buffalo and ox remains — showing the spread of agriculture into the eastern Gangetic plain.

nodes.label: Early Burials
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Several burial sites found at Mehrgarh where dead were buried with goats, probably meant as food in the afterlife. Indicates belief in life after death and social rituals around death.

nodes.label: Cotton Cultivation
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Cotton was probably grown at Mehrgarh from about 7000 years ago. Actual cloth pieces were found attached to objects at Mohenjodaro. Spindle whorls of terracotta and faience were used to spin thread.

nodes.label: Lower Palaeolithic
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Earliest phase of the Stone Age. Globally begins ~2.6 million BCE (Oldowan); in India it is not older than ~600,000 BCE, with Bori (Maharashtra) being the earliest known Lower Palaeolithic site. In India the phase runs ~600,000–150,000 BCE. Characterised by hand axes, cleavers, and choppers (Acheulian and pre-Acheulian traditions). Associated with Homo erectus and Homo habilis. Indian sites: Bori, Soan/Sohan valley (Punjab/Pakistan), Belan valley (UP), Didwana (Rajasthan), Nagarjunakonda (AP), Bhimbetka (lower layers), Attirampakkam (TN), Hunsgi (Karnataka), Chirki-Nevasa (Maharashtra, 2000 tools). People were primarily food-gatherers with small-game hunting.

nodes.label: Middle Palaeolithic
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Middle phase of the Stone Age. In India, ~150,000–35,000 BCE. Tools become smaller and more refined — flakes rather than cores (Levallois technique). Principal tools: blades, points, borers, scrapers, all made from flakes. Associated with Neanderthals globally and archaic Homo sapiens. Indian sites: Narmada valley, Nevasa (Maharashtra), Didwana (Rajasthan), Belan valley (UP), and several south of Tungabhadra river. The Belan valley has stone tools plus animal fossils (cattle, deer).

nodes.label: Upper Palaeolithic
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Final phase of the Stone Age. In India, ~35,000–10,000 BCE, with 566 sites identified. Characterised by blade-and-burin tools and the first bone tools. Earliest cave/rock art appears (Bhimbetka upper layers, Lascaux globally). Associated with modern Homo sapiens sapiens. Sites in AP, Karnataka, Maharashtra, central MP, southern UP, Jharkhand, Gujarat sand dunes. Earliest Upper Palaeolithic site in the subcontinent: Fa Hien Cave (Sri Lanka, ~31,000 BCE artefacts). Climate was less humid during this phase (last phase of the ice age).

nodes.label: Pre-Cultural Hominins
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Era before stone tools, when the hominin lineage emerged and diversified. Spans from the chimpanzee–hominin split (~6–7 million years ago) to the earliest Oldowan stone tools (~2.6 million years ago). Key developments: bipedalism, early Australopithecus species (e.g. Lucy, Australopithecus afarensis at ~3.2 mya in Ethiopia). No material culture yet — recognised only through fossils. Ends with the emergence of Homo habilis and the first flaked stone tools.

nodes.label: Chalcolithic
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Copper-Stone Age: cultures using copper and stone implements together (low-grade bronze and occasional iron appear too). In India, spans c. 3000-500 BCE with strong regional variation - technologically, the Chalcolithic stage applies to pre-Harappan cultures, but in many regions Chalcolithic cultures in fact followed the Bronze Age Harappan. Chalcolithic peoples were primarily rural (contrast: the Harappans urbanized using Indus flood-plain surplus). Key Indian Chalcolithic cultures and type-sites: Ahar-Banas (Rajasthan, type-sites: Ahar, Gilund; c. 2100-1500 BCE); Kayatha (Malwa, MP; c. 2000-1800 BCE); Malwa (Navdatoli/Eran/Nagda; 1700-1200 BCE); Jorwe (Maharashtra, type-site Jorwe; major settlements Daimabad and Inamgaon; c. 1400-700 BCE); Prabhas-Rangpur (Gujarat). Characteristic pottery: black-and-red ware (from ~2000 BCE), often painted with white linear designs.

nodes.label: Jogimara Caves
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Ancient caves in the Ramgarh hills, Surguja district of Chhattisgarh. Paintings dated to around 1000 BCE. Contains what is often described as the world's oldest theatre/amphitheatre room — murals in this room mark a transition between prehistoric rock art and historic-period murals. Adorn a non-sacred space (the theatre), unusual for paintings of this era.

nodes.label: Mirzapur Rock Paintings
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Prehistoric rock paintings in the Vindhyan sandstone shelters of Mirzapur district, southern Uttar Pradesh. Among the standard-reference sites for Indian rock art alongside Bhimbetka and Panchmarhi. Paintings span Mesolithic to Chalcolithic with hunting and everyday-life themes.

nodes.label: Panchmarhi
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Pachmarhi (also Panchmarhi) in the Satpura range of Madhya Pradesh. Contains extensive prehistoric rock paintings spanning Upper Palaeolithic to Chalcolithic. Key reference site for Indian rock art alongside Bhimbetka and Mirzapur. Also MP's only hill station.

nodes.label: Petroglyphs
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Rock engravings — images carved, chipped, or abraded into stone surfaces. Distinct from rock paintings (which use pigments applied to the rock). A key prehistoric art technique, often found alongside paintings at the same sites (including Bhimbetka). The term covers all forms of physical rock-surface marking as opposed to painted rock art.

nodes.label: Inamgaon
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: A major Chalcolithic settlement of the Jorwe culture in Pune district, Maharashtra, on the Ghod river (a tributary of the Bhima). Along with Daimabad, one of the two Jorwe-culture sites that had almost reached the urban stage. Had specialist craftsmen - potters, smiths, ivory carvers, lime makers - and evidence of social stratification visible in house types: some elites in large rectangular houses, others in round huts. Features a large chief's house, possibly used for storing tributes in kind. Burials included adults interred with pottery and copper goods.

nodes.label: Ahar
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Type-site of the Ahar culture in the dry Banas valley of southeastern Rajasthan (near Udaipur). Original name: Tambavati ('place of copper'). People here practised smelting and metallurgy from the outset, producing flat copper axes, bangles, and sheets. Unusually for a Chalcolithic site, Ahar virtually used no microlithic tools - stone axes and blades are essentially absent. Dated c. 2100-1500 BCE. Spread over about 4 hectares. Along with Gilund (a regional centre), these are the two major Ahar-culture sites.

nodes.label: Kayatha
nodes.subject: history
nodes.detail: Type-site of the Kayatha culture in Malwa (western Madhya Pradesh), near Ujjain. Dated c. 2000-1800 BCE, coexisting with the late phase of the Harappan civilisation. Shows both pre-Harappan and Harappan influences in its pottery. Notable find: one house yielded twenty-nine copper bangles and two unique copper axes - evidence of metal accumulation by specific households. Along with Eran, one of the earliest Chalcolithic settlements of central India; Kayatha was later superseded at the same region by the Ahar culture and then the Malwa culture.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Ramapithecus & Sivapithecus
nodes.detail: Early hominid skulls found in the Siwalik hills (India–Pakistan border region) — specifically in the Potwar plateau of Pakistani Punjab (developed on sandstone). Dated ~2.2 million years ago. Ramapithecus was female; both belonged to the same group. Possess some hominid features but represent apes. A related Greek fossil is dated ~10 million years ago. This Siwalik hominid line came to a dead end in the subcontinent — became extinct without spreading further.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Hathnora (Narmada Man)
nodes.detail: A site in the middle valley of the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh where an almost-complete fossilized hominid skull was discovered in 1982. Initially called Homo erectus, now anatomically recognised as archaic Homo sapiens. The most significant hominid fossil find in India — evidence that archaic humans inhabited central India in the Middle Pleistocene (~700,000 BCE). Often called 'Narmada Man'.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Bori (Maharashtra)
nodes.detail: Site in Maharashtra considered the earliest Lower Palaeolithic site in the Indian subcontinent (~600,000 BCE). Bori artefacts give the starting date for the Indian Lower Palaeolithic. Establishes that while Lower Palaeolithic began ~2 million years ago in Africa, in India it is no older than ~600,000 years.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Soan Valley
nodes.detail: Valley of the Son/Sohan river in Punjab (now Pakistan) — classic Lower Palaeolithic site of the subcontinent. Yielded early stone tools (hand axes, cleavers, choppers) of the Acheulian tradition. Along with Kashmir and the Thar desert, forms one of the best-known Early Old Stone Age regions of the subcontinent.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Belan Valley
nodes.detail: Valley in southern Uttar Pradesh at the foothills of the Vindhyas. Rich in stone tools and animal fossils (cattle, deer). Contains evidence spanning both Lower and Middle Palaeolithic ages, making it an important multi-period archaeological landscape.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Didwana (Paleo)
nodes.detail: A desert site in Rajasthan (distinct from the Didwana saline lake of modern geography). Yielded stone tools of all three Palaeolithic phases — Lower, Middle, and Upper — a rare stratified record making it key for understanding the progression of stone tool technologies in western India.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Fa Hien Cave
nodes.detail: Cave in Sri Lanka with fossils of Homo sapiens sapiens (modern humans) dated ~34,000 years old; artefacts ~31,000 years old. Earliest Upper Palaeolithic site in the Indian subcontinent. Supports the hypothesis that the earliest modern humans arrived in India via an early coastal migration from Africa ~50,000 years ago — from the south, not the north.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Bagor
nodes.detail: Well-excavated Mesolithic site in Rajasthan. Distinctive microlithic industry. Inhabitants subsisted on hunting and pastoralism. Occupied continuously for 5,000 years from the 5th millennium BCE onwards. Along with Adamgarh (MP), provides the earliest evidence for animal domestication in India (~5000 BCE).

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Adamgarh
nodes.detail: Mesolithic site in Madhya Pradesh. Along with Bagor (Rajasthan), provides the earliest evidence for the domestication of animals in the Indian part of the subcontinent (~5000 BCE). Key site for understanding the transition from hunting-gathering to pastoralism in central India.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.chapter_title: Human Evolution: The Old Stone Age
nodes.label: Sambhar
nodes.detail: A former salt lake in Rajasthan whose deposits suggest plant cultivation in the region as early as 7000–6000 BCE — earliest evidence of plant cultivation in India. Important for understanding the transition from gathering to agriculture at the Mesolithic–Neolithic interface.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.label: Gufkral
nodes.detail: Neolithic site 41 km south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir. Name means 'cave of the potter'. People practised both agriculture and animal husbandry. Part of the Kashmiri Neolithic group along with Burzahom — distinguished by pit dwellings, wide ceramic range, stone and bone tools, and the complete absence of microliths.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.label: Piklihal
nodes.detail: Important Neolithic site in Karnataka. Inhabitants were cattle-herders who domesticated cattle, sheep, and goats. Set up seasonal camps surrounded by cowpens made of posts and stakes; accumulated dung which was burned when abandoning camp — producing the characteristic 'ash mounds' of the south Indian Neolithic. Both ash mounds and habitation sites have been excavated.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.label: Brahmagiri
nodes.detail: Neolithic site in Karnataka. Part of the southern Neolithic group (850+ settlements across AP, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu). Also known for later occupation including Iron Age and Ashokan Minor Rock Edict. The south-Indian Neolithic phase covered c. 2400–1000 BCE.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.label: Maski
nodes.detail: Neolithic site in Karnataka (southern Neolithic group). Famously also the site of a Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka — the first edict where Ashoka's personal name 'Devanampiya Asoka' was identified, confirming the identity of 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' mentioned in other edicts as Ashoka Maurya.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.label: Hallur
nodes.detail: Neolithic site in Karnataka (southern group). Notable for yielding some of the earliest evidence of iron in India (~1200 BCE in its later layers), marking the Neolithic-to-Iron-Age transition in peninsular India. Part of the same cluster as Maski, Brahmagiri, and Piklihal.

nodes.subject: history
nodes.label: Senuwar
nodes.detail: Important Neolithic site in the Rohtas district of Bihar, in the Kaimur hilly area. Part of the eastern Neolithic group along with Taradih (near the Bodh-Gaya temple). Shows Neolithic settlement patterns in eastern India.
